title: The Machinist
full_review:
In director Brad Anderson's darkly arresting psychological thriller "The Machinist" (Paramount Classics), Christian Bale plays Trevor Reznik, a skeletal lathe operator suffering from chronic insomnia whose fragile psyche is edged toward madness by the presence of a mysterious and menacing co-worker (John Sharian).

Reznik's frayed mental state is further unraveled by cryptic notes that appear on his home refrigerator and unnerving flashes of deja vu. After a grisly job-related accident, his co-workers turn against him, fueling his paranoia. Reznik only finds solace in the companionship of a sympathetic coffee-shop waitress (Aitana Sanchez-Gijon) and a comforting call girl (Jennifer Jason Leigh).

Anderson has crafted a grimly stylish and suspenseful meditation on guilt, alienation and paranoia, dripping with nightmarish atmospherics and noir moodiness, buttressed by Roque Banos' Bernard Herrmann-inspired score.

Filmed in creepy, washed-out tones for added bleak effect, the movie, though unremittingly cheerless, ends on a redemptive note.
Bale, who lost a jaw-dropping 63 pounds for the role, is mesmerizing. With his gaunt face and protruding rib cage, he looks like he stepped out of a concentration camp. But it is what goes on behind his hollow eyes that gives his performance its intensity.

Due to several instances of violence, including a gruesome amputation, sexual situations with nudity, and recurring rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
